references.text: Pharaoh was warned about the locust plague, and here we see that his servants persuaded him to call Moses and Aaron back for negotiations.
Pharaoh had previously given partial permission for the Israelites to sacrifice, but with restrictions. Here he again asks who should go.
Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh for the first time with the demand to let the people go to serve their God, the same demand that is repeated here.
Pharaoh's answer to the question of who should go - he would only let the men leave, not the whole people.
After the tenth plague, Pharaoh finally gave full permission for all Israel to go and serve the Lord.
The Lord's command through Moses to Pharaoh to let the people go so they could serve him, the same message behind Pharaoh's question here.
The connection between God's direct command to Moses and Pharaoh's response using the same wording underscores the continuity of the conflict's core.
The verses form a direct dialogue sequence where Pharaoh tries to negotiate his way out of full liberation by changing who should go.
This verse highlights the repeated pattern in Pharaoh's negotiations: he offers partial freedom with conditions, which underscores his unwillingness to fully obey.
The link between the early prophetic instruction and later confrontations confirms that 'service' is the purpose of the exodus from the very beginning.
This strong contrast between refusal in chapter 5 and invitation in chapter 10 illustrates Pharaoh's gradual downfall and God's unchanging demand.
The connection shows how Pharaoh, even after admitting sin, still tries to manipulate the outcome by questioning who should go.
